Let  

\[
p = \text{price of the pen (in CHF)} .
\]

Then the price of the book is  

\[
p+1 = \text{price of the book}.
\]

The total cost is  

\[
p + (p+1)=1{,}10 .
\]

Solve for \(p\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
p + p + 1 &= 1{,}10 \\
2p + 1 &= 1{,}10 \\
2p &= 1{,}10 - 1 \\
2p &= 0{,}10 \\
p &= \frac{0{,}10}{2}=0{,}05 .
\end{aligned}
\]

So the pen costs **0.05 CHF**, i.e. **5 centesimi**.

---

### Why 10 centesimi doesn’t work  

If the pen were 10 centesimi, its price would be \([0{,}10]\), and the book, which costs 1 CHF more, would be  

\([0{,}10 + 1{,}00] = \$1{,}10\) (in centesimi: 110 centesimi).  

The sum would then be  

\(10 + 110 = 120 \text{centesimi}\), which is more than the required 110 centesimi.  

Hence the intuition of 10 centesimi is too high; the correct cost is 5 centesimi.  

\[
\boxed{5\text{ centesimi}}
\]

Equation: p + (p + 1) = 1.10

=> 2p + 1 = 1.10

=> 2p = 0.10

=> p = 0.05 CHF = 5 centesimi.

Thus answer: 5 centesimi.
